As shown in the figure above, first, rope_params determines how far to rotate each pair, returning two “tables” that store the cosine and sine of those angles. Or, in other words, rope_params computes the cosine and sine of each rotation angle, which depends on the token’s position and the feature pair’s frequency.

import torch def rope_params(head_dim, positions, base=10_000): assert head_dim % 2 == 0 indices = torch.arange(0, head_dim, 2, device=positions.device) inv_freq = base ** (-indices.float() / head_dim) angles = positions.float()[:, None] * inv_freq[None, :] return angles.cos(), angles.sin()

The indices array in the rope_params function contains the 2i values from the frequency formula in Section 4:

For our eight-feature query, the indicesare [0, 2, 4, 6], that is, one 2i value for each feature pair. Suppose we use the common base b = 10,000. And following our earlier examples, we choose a small head dimension of d = 8. In this case, the inv_freq then computes the four pair frequencies θi = b−2i/d as follows:

As we can see above, the resulting inv_freq has one frequency θi for each of the four feature pairs ( measured in radians) per token position.

Next, the angles then multiplies each pair’s frequency θi with the token position m, which computes the rotation angle mθi. In our example, with positions = [2], we get:

Finally, rope_params takes the cosine and sine of each angle and outputs them as two so-called cosine and sine tables, cos and sin. In both tables, each row is a token position and each column is a feature pair. Since we only use token position 2 here, each table has shape (1, 4), with the single row shown below:

For the example in Figure 26, each table has one row for token position 2 and four columns, one for each feature pair. Figure 27 shows the rotation angle for each pair and the corresponding entries in the two tables.

In short, rope_params computes the cosine and sine of each rotation angle, which depends on the token’s position and the feature pair’s frequency.

In a real-world scenario, if we pass rope_params 1,024 token positions for a context size of 1024, and a head dimension of 128, it returns two tensors, cos and sin, each with shape (1024, 64) since a head with 128 features has 64 pairs.

The tables have no batch or head dimension, and we broadcast each (1024, 64) table across the batch and head dimensions. So, if we have multi-head attention or grouped query attention with 32 heads, feature pair 0 at token position 2 uses the same rotation angle in all 32 heads. Each head rotates its own feature values, so the rotated queries can still differ across heads. Also, the same entries can be reused across queries, keys, and heads that use the same positions and frequencies. In short, we only need to (pre)compute these tables once per model for all positions up to a maximum supported context size.

Technically, it would also be possible to store these tables alongside the model weights; but they are so incredibly cheap to compute that storing them on disk would be overkill.

Next, rope_split_half uses those cosines and sines to rotate the actual features in the query and key vectors inside attention.

def rope_split_half(x, cos, sin): first, second = x.float().chunk(2, dim=-1) return torch.cat(( first * cos - second * sin, first * sin + second * cos, ), dim=-1).to(x.dtype)

Considering the simple 8-feature example once more, the .chunk in the code snippet above splits the query into [1, 2, 3, 4] and [5, 6, 7, 8] and lines up the two entries in each pair. For example, the first slot of each half gives us (1, 5), the second (2, 6), and so on. The two expressions inside torch.cat compute the rotated halves using the equations from Section 3.3:

Note that here, everything denoted with ai corresponds to the first half of the query, and everything denoted with bi comes from the second half. The first expression inside torch.cat computes all the ai′values, and the second computes all the bi′ values.

Then, we concatenate the halves, which puts each value back in its original index position via torch.cat.

Here’s the code that produces the rotated query in the earlier Figure 26. The shown reshape (1, 1, 1, 8) just brings the simple toy array into the expected format: one batch item, one head, one token, and eight features.

positions = torch.tensor([2]) cos, sin = rope_params(8, positions) q = torch.arange(1., 9.).reshape(1, 1, 1, 8) q_rot = rope_split_half(q, cos, sin) print(q_rot[0, 0, 0])

With several positions, each token simply picks up its own row from the cos and sin tables. Through broadcasting, PyTorch reuses these same tables across all batch items and attention heads.

5.2 Using RoPE inside causal attention

So far, we coded the RoPE utility functions. Let’s now use it in the real context, the attention mechanism. Here, we use the standard frequency schedule for two 8-feature heads and four token positions. We use random query, key, and value tensors to keep the example self-contained, but as mentioned before, you can optionally also check the end-to-end Qwen3 from-scratch implementation with real query, key, and values produced by the pre-trained model.

torch.manual_seed(123) q = torch.randn(1, 2, 4, 8) # 1 batch, 2 heads, 4 tokens, 8 head dim k = torch.randn(1, 2, 4, 8) v = torch.randn(1, 2, 4, 8) positions = torch.arange(4) cos, sin = rope_params(8, positions) q_rot = rope_split_half(q, cos, sin) k_rot = rope_split_half(k, cos, sin) scores = q_rot @ k_rot.transpose(-2, -1) / q.shape[-1] ** 0.5 future_mask = positions[None, :] > positions[:, None] masked_scores = scores.masked_fill(future_mask, -torch.inf) weights = torch.softmax(masked_scores, dim=-1) context = weights @ v

Note that only q and k but not v pass through RoPE. The resulting raw attention scores are stored in a tensor of shape (1, 2, 4, 4), that is, one row for each query position, and a column for each key position, and 4x4 since we have four tokens where each attends to each other.

Then, using a conventional attention code implementation, the causal mask replaces the scores for future keys with negative infinity, so they get zeroed after the softmax. The resulting context tensor has shape (1, 2, 4, 8); the 4 because we have four tokens, and the 8 because the embedding dimension was originally 8.

We can also check that our claim about relative offsets holds, meaning that adding 3 to each position should change the position but preserve the query-key offsets:

cos_shifted, sin_shifted = rope_params(8, positions + 3) q_shifted = rope_split_half(q, cos_shifted, sin_shifted) k_shifted = rope_split_half(k, cos_shifted, sin_shifted) scores_shifted = ( q_shifted @ k_shifted.transpose(-2, -1) / q.shape[-1] ** 0.5 ) torch.testing.assert_close(scores, scores_shifted) # Should return True 5.3 An alternative feature-pairing convention

I mentioned the split-halves convention many times throughout this article. The original RoPE paper uses the alternative interleaved convention, as does the original LLaMA implementation (but as mentioned before, most code implementations now use the split-halves, because it makes it easier, in code, to rotate all pairs at once with element-wise sine and cosine operations.)

To illustrate the difference between the two layouts, Figure 28 below uses the same 8-feature vector in both rows.

The interleaved implementation uses the same two equations, but selects alternating features and interleaves the outputs.

def rope_interleaved(x, cos, sin): even, odd = x.float()[..., 0::2], x.float()[..., 1::2] return torch.stack(( even * cos - odd * sin, even * sin + odd * cos, ), dim=-1).flatten(-2).to(x.dtype)

But mathematically, the layouts are equivalent when we account for the feature order. So, rearranging the entries [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] to [1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8] makes the split-half pairs adjacent with pairs (1, 5), (2, 6), and so on. If we apply the same rearrangement to both queries and keys, it results in identical dot products.

order = torch.tensor([0, 4, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7], device=q.device) q_rot_interleaved = rope_interleaved(q[..., order], cos, sin) k_rot_interleaved = rope_interleaved(k[..., order], cos, sin) scores_interleaved = ( q_rot_interleaved @ k_rot_interleaved.transpose(-2, -1) / q.shape[-1] ** 0.5 ) torch.testing.assert_close(q_rot[..., order], q_rot_interleaved) torch.testing.assert_close(k_rot[..., order], k_rot_interleaved) torch.testing.assert_close(scores, scores_interleaved) # This should all return True

The outputs retain the reordered features, so we compare them with the split-half outputs in that same order. Applying the two layouts to the original vector however would give different scores.

6. Positional choices in modern architectures

RoPE has been a staple in most (open-weight) LLMs since the original LLaMA model. Of course, proprietary models may use it as well, but it’s always hard to say anything with 100% certainty about proprietary models.

However, in recent years, many architectures have been moving away from full-blown RoPE in every transformer block. In the following subsection, we will discuss some of these variants.

For instance the full RoPE implementation we discussed and implemented in the sections above rotates every feature pair in every query and key head.

In the following examples in the subsections above below, we will see that models only rotate some features within a head, other models skip RoPE in some transformer blocks, and some models use a different approach and add position information directly to their attention scores.

6.1 Partial RoPE

As discussed throughout the article, regular “full” RoPE rotates all dimensions in each query and key head. Partial RoPE is a variant that rotates only a subset, while leaving the remaining dimensions unchanged.

For example, MiniMax-M3’s configuration uses 64 rotary dimensions within each 128-dimensional head. That gives 32 rotated feature pairs and 64 unchanged dimensions. The figure below illustrates how that looks like.

Note that if we look past the first transformer block, the unrotated features can still contain position information inherited from earlier transformer blocks.

Anyways, what’s the point behind partial RoPE? It saves some memory. For example, in the MiniMax-M3 example above, rotating half the features reduces the size of the precomputed cosine and sine tables also in half. So, with partial RoPE, instead of 64 columns, now each table only needs 32 columns. However, note that the KV cache still stores the full key and value vectors for each cached token.

For MiniMax-M3’s 1M-token context, rotating 64 of the 128 features halves the size of the precomputed cosine and sine tables, saving 0.134 GB (128 MiB) if the tables are stored in BF16. If the tables themselves were stored in NVFP4, the savings would be 0.038 GB (36 MiB), including the block scales.

Note that in experiments with 1B to 8B models, the Fractional Rotation, Full Potential? paper found that rotating around 10% of each head’s features often gave similar training loss and benchmark accuracy to full RoPE. However, full RoPE did better on some evaluations.

So, in my opinion, partial RoPE is hardly worth it.

6.2 NoPE layers

NoPE was coined in the The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers paper and means no explicit positional encoding. The idea or observation is that an attention layer without any explicit position method still has a causal mask, where a query can attend only to itself and earlier tokens. And this causal masking implicitly provides positional information.

Let’s use the first four tokens from our earlier example, The red fox jumps. In Figure 30, the query for fox at position 2 can attend to The, red, and itself. The query for red at position 1 can attend to The and itself.

So, the next question is how can the model use the causal mask as a position signal? Here’s a toy example adapted from the paper.

Suppose one feature of the value vectors is 1 for The and 0 for the other three tokens. Since the input only contains only one The, every visible prefix contains exactly one 1. If all non-masked keys get the same attention score, the softmax assigns every visible token equal weight.

So at fox, attention averages 1, 0, and 0, which gives 1/3. At jumps, it averages four values and gets 1/4. In other words, this output feature equals one over the prefix length, which a later layer can use as a signal for position.

Does NoPE work in practice? The researchers of the NoPE paper trained a tiny 107M-parameter decoder-only transformers from scratch on tasks such as copying, sorting, and addition to do some ablation.

When they tested the small model on examples longer than those seen during training, interestingly, NoPE ranked first overall across the ten tasks and ahead of RoPE. The researchers behind the NoPE paper also conducted a separate experiment with a larger 1.3B-parameter models trained on code. Here, NoPE also handled contexts beyond the training length, however, its next-token predictions got worse at the longest lengths tested.

Some of today’s open-weight LLMs even go so far and use NoPE in all layers. However, nowadays, it’s more common for models to omit RoPE in at least some layers, where layer here means transformer block.

To give a concrete example, SmolLM3 (3B parameters) applies RoPE in three layers and skips it in the fourth, repeating that pattern through 36 layers. Interestingly, the SmolLM3 authors mentioned that this layer pattern improved long-context performance.

(Also note that any later layer, following the first one, even though it may skip the rotation, still receives the inputs from preceding transformer blocks, so its queries and keys still receive some sort of position information from earlier layers.)

6.3 Learned relative position bias

Before we get to the overview and look at what modern architectures use, there’s one more method to introduce. For instance, Thinky’s Inkling uses a learned relative position bias in both its sliding-window and global attention layers. It computes the usual scaled dot product between a query and key, and then it adds a certain number to that score before the softmax in the attention score computation. That number depends on the query token’s hidden state and how many positions back the key is.

Let’s reuse our example sentence, “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” (It’s the last time, I promise!) In the figure below, the “the” at position 5 is the query and “fox” at position 2 is the key. Inkling then uses the three-position gap between query and key and the hidden state for “the” to compute the bias, then adds it to the scaled dot product.

This is not an entirely new idea. Some of you may recall Google’s popular T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) in 2019, which used a simpler version of this idea.

6.4 How these choices appear in recent models

Now, after all this build up, the interesting question is: which architecture uses which method? And what are the recent trends?

To answer this, I grouped the entries in my LLM Architecture Gallery by their listed release dates and compared the 2025 releases with the earlier and later releases in the 2026 snapshot. Each gallery card counts once, so multiple variants of an architecture can contribute to the results. LLM Architecture Gallery

As we can see in Figure 35 above, using RoPE in every softmax attention layer is still the most common choice. However, its use fell from 2025 to 2026, and then also in the latter half of 2026, which could be a trend.

Consequently, there is a growing number of models that mix RoPE and NoPE. The groups are still small, so it’s hard to say whether these trends will continue.

The NoPE only entries were all recurrent hybrids with softmax attention layers that use no explicit positional encoding. The “Other” category here refers to xLSTM 7B (2025) and Inkling (2026). xLSTM has no softmax attention layers. Inkling adds a learned bias to the attention scores before softmax, as we saw in Section 6.3.

Among the models that use RoPE, partial RoPE became more common from 2025 to 2026. It went from a minority of the RoPE models in 2025 to a majority in both 2026 groups, as shown in Figure 36.

If you’d like to look up an individual model from the 2026 groups, Figure 37 below shows the 2026 gallery overview with the individual architectures labeled by position type. You can also browse the gallery interactively here.

7. Final thoughts

So, to recap, we discussed GPT-2 and the original transformer that add a position vector to each token embedding before the first transformer block. Then, modern LLMs switched to RoPE, which encodes relative position inside attention by rotating queries and keys. Surprisingly, RoPE remains as the most popular positional embedding method today.

Recently, however, Inkling picked up an idea from T5 to add a learned relative position bias to the attention scores before softmax. And then we also have NoPE-RoPE architectures, which omit RoPE in some layers.

It may be boring news, but as mentioned before, RoPE is still the predominant position embedding method, and I think this will carry over into 2027 for sure. Perhaps, though, we’ll see more architectures with an Inkling-like design coming up in 2027.

While this may sound “boring”, I am glad that I finally got this article on RoPE (and other position info methods) out, after so many years, so that I can add it to my collection of LLM “fundamentals” explainers.

If you are interested in the other architecture building blocks of LLMs, I still highly recommend starting with a GPT-2-style model, which will give you a solid understanding of the building blocks with the least amount of friction. And from there, you can then layer on additional methods (such as RoPE).

If you’d like to build that GPT-2-style model yourself, my first Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book walks through all the building blocks depicted in the figure below.

For the methods that branch off from the GPT-2 baseline, I’ve collected some of my relevant blog articles below, starting with a refresher on self-attention:

Self-attention, causal masking, and multi-head attention: Understanding and Coding Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Causal-Attention, and Cross-Attention in LLMs

Modern attention variants (GQA, MLA, sliding-window attention, sparse attention, and hybrids): A Visual Guide to Attention Variants in Modern LLMs

The KV cache. Understanding and Coding the KV Cache in LLMs from Scratch

SwiGLU feed-forward layers and normalization (LayerNorm and RMSNorm): From GPT-2 to gpt-oss: Analyzing the Architectural Advances

Mixture-of-experts layers and expert routing. The Big LLM Architecture Comparison

Residual connections and DeepSeek’s manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC): Recent Developments in LLM Architectures: KV Sharing, mHC, and Compressed Attention

Putting some of the pieces together in Qwen3: Understanding and Implementing Qwen3 From Scratch walks through implementing the dense and mixture-of-experts versions in PyTorch.

Thanks for reading and supporting my work!

PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.

entry.title: A NES emulator written in Odin
entry.content:
I made a NES emulator in Odin!

Intro

I’ve started this project in late June of 2024. I’ve worked on it in my spare time off and on. I decided to put a pause on this project in January 2025 to focus on other things.

I’ve learned so much about:

The NES architecture, and possibly about game console architectures in general Bits and bytes, hex notation, and bitwise operations. The Odin programming language. I haven’t used it on a serious project before. How computers work. CPU instructions, “cycles”, etc Emulation. It’s very hard. Respect to emulator developers!

It’s been a wild ride. I’ve had a lot of fun, but I’ve also suffered more towards the end, when trying to make the emulator “fully” accurate.

You can read the Github Readme for more info about the project.

Features Enough emulation accuracy to run Battletoads and hundreds of other games perfectly. Debugger view with some debugging features Menu view to interact with the emulator Save states Controller support CRT Shader toggle (Partial) Sound Supported Mappers: NROM, MMC1, UXROM, CNROM, MMC3, GxROM, AxROM Making an emulator

I’ve seen some people say that making a NES emulator is a simple weekend project, and I frankly found that baffling. Because evidently, it’s not. It took me 7 months to get my emulator to how it is now.

I think what they actually mean is that getting a NES emulator “working” takes a short time. Like maybe getting Donkey Kong to run. And that’s true. You can get to 80% or maybe 90% pretty fast. It’s the last 10% that takes a long, long time.

The NES hardware has many idiosyncrasies that need to be emulated for certain games to run. Many games depend on very specific NES behavior. And if you don’t implement it right, they won’t run. A lot of the challenge is about timing. The CPU and the PPU (the chip that handles the graphics rendering in the NES) run in parallel and they communicate with each other. That timing needs to be very accurate, or many wrong things can happen. Most games will run fine with a less than accurate emulator, but a lot of them won’t, and they will need you to consider things in more detail.

Another issue is mappers. Mappers are what we call an implementation of a type of cartridge. You see, NES games come in cartridges, and cartridges aren’t just data. They are circuitry with their own behavior and extra resources like read-only memory, and writable memory. Some come with extra audio capabilities, but I haven’t implemented that.

Anyway, you have to implement these mappers if you want a game that comes in that cartridge to run in your game. They complete the NES’s circuitry. In a way, they are a part of the NES hardware. There are many mappers, but you can support a lot of games by just implementing a few. I’ve had trouble implementing some mappers, and some of them are still badly implemented, causing some games to not work. I found it hard to understand some of the mapper documentation.

The biggest challenge with making an emulator, I think, is to know what to implement. Information about the hardware, and what needs to be emulated about the hardware for games to work in your emulator. Thankfully, the NES is very well documented online. I’ve used many resources, like:

The Nesdev wiki The nesdev wiki discord. People here have helped me with my issues a lot. Javidx’s NES series. The code has many mistakes but it’s a good starting point. This article about the NES’s PPU Test ROMS. These NES ROMS thoroughly test particular aspects of your emulator. This is an extraordinary tool to accelerate development of emulator accuracy.

I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without these resources and the help from people in the nesdev discord.

Odin

I’ve learned a lot about Odin while making this project. I think it fit this project like a glove. Being a very simple, strongly typed C-like language that gives me all the freedom I want makes making an emulator much easier than using other languages, I feel.

One thing that threw me off was that Odin has no automatic integer promotion. When doing calculations on numbers, Odin will never promote types to a bigger one. That led to a few bugs. But I blame this all on me and me being used to C’s integer promotion.

One fun thing that I’ve learned was doing a bit of memory allocation strategy. Odin has no automatic memory management, so you have to come up with smart ways to handle memory. I’ve had fun thinking about how I should handle memory best. I didn’t need to do anything complicated. I mostly use one temporary allocator that clears every frame, a global heap allocator for things that need to live forever, and a NES Arena allocator for anything that needs to live along a NES session. I found memory allocation fun.

Another thing I had to learn is how to serialize Odin objects. I used the CBOR library, and I ran into a few issues. I thought my code was misbehaving due to a bug in the library, but that was cleared up. It was only having trouble because I made a few odd types that it didn’t know how to serialize. Once I learned how to properly write custom handling for types, everything worked perfectly. This was one of the tricky types that cbor didn’t know how to serialize:

PpuCtrl :: struct #raw_union { // VPHB SINN using flags: bit_field u8 { n: u8 | 2, i: u8 | 1, s: u8 | 1, // sprite pattern table address for 8x8 sprites (0: $0000, 1: $1000) b: u8 | 1, // bg pattern table address (0: $0000, 1: $1000) h: u8 | 1, // sprite size (0: 8x8, 1: 8x16) p: u8 | 1, v: u8 | 1, // vblank NMI enable }, reg:         u8, }

I love how Odin lets you define raw unions like this, and with bit fields. It fits emulator development very well.

What’s missing

I don’t consider this project “finished”. Of course, a project like this is never truly finished, but a lot of aspects of it need a lot of work, for sure:

The sound. lucyNES doesn’t sound very well still. Some games will sound fine but most won’t. I have to improve the implementation, and implement the DMC channel which I haven’t done. Some games that I’ve tested don’t work due to a poor mapper implementation I could implement more mappers so more games are supported.

These are the main things that are lacking at this moment. Maybe at some point I will return and keep working on this so the project can feel “complete”.

entry.title: The MacBook Pro's OLED PWM problem
entry.content:
The MacBook Pro’s OLED PWM Problem: When a ‘Better’ Display Becomes Worse to Use

Apple has made a spectacular display. But spectacular isn’t the same as comfortable, and the people discovering that distinction deserve to be heard.

Apple has brought tandem OLED technology to the MacBook Pro, joining the Mini-LED display that has served the range since 2021 (and which Apple continues to sell). Apple calls this a “PROLED XDR Display”. It features individually illuminated pixels, effectively infinite contrast, wonderfully deep blacks and the sort of image quality that Mini-LED, for all its considerable strengths, can’t fully equal. Peak HDR brightness has increased, and Apple has introduced a new display engine designed to manage colour, luminance and pixel usage with extraordinary precision. And of course, in a first for any Apple notebook display, it has touch-input capability.

When Apple unveiled the new MacBook Pro, the initial reaction to the screen was overwhelmingly positive.

But there’s a burgeoning discussion taking place within the Mac community that deserves attention. On MacRumors forums, a thread titled RIP MacBook Pro PROLED for PWM Sensitive Eyes - apple cmon! has attracted people describing remarkably similar experiences. Discussions are also appearing across Reddit, with owners describing discomfort shortly after using their new machines. Some report headaches; others describe a strange sensation of eye fatigue, dizziness, nausea, or an inability to concentrate on the screen for extended periods. Some have already returned the device.

Mike Wuerthele, of AppleInsider, published an article on 10 November titled If you’re getting dizzy using PROLED MacBook Pro, you are not alone, examining these reports.

The following caveat probably doesn't need to be made, but I will make it anyway: these are individual experiences, not evidence that the new MacBook Pro is causing problems for everyone. Plenty of owners are likely perfectly content with (and dazzled by) their new displays. But that isn’t really the point. For the people experiencing these symptoms, the fact that somebody else can happily spend several hours staring at the same screen isn’t particularly reassuring, especially given Apple's long-standing commitment to accessibility. A display can be technically spectacular and still be a spectacularly poor display for a subset of people.

PWM

Much of the discussion centres on Pulse Width Modulation, or PWM. It’s a technique used to control screen brightness by rapidly switching or modulating the light output. On an OLED display, the pixels themselves produce the light, rather than relying on a separate backlight. By varying the way that light output is modulated, the display can control its apparent brightness.

At sufficiently high frequencies, this flickering isn’t something most people can consciously detect. But some people are particularly sensitive to this kind of modulation and can experience eye strain, headaches and other forms of discomfort when looking at displays that use it.

This is a pretty good demonstration of PWM on an M4 iPad Pro, which also has a tandem OLED display:

Neither PWM nor the discussion surrounding it is new. It’s been a talking point for years, particularly around OLED displays, and something manufacturers have increasingly had to consider as display technology has evolved (including Apple — more on this later).

Notebookcheck, which conducted laboratory testing of the 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, measured PWM at 240Hz. This is its worst-case reading, with flickering detected at brightness settings of 99% and below.

To put that into perspective, the M4 Pro MacBook Pro with Mini-LED display measured 14,880Hz in Notebookcheck’s testing. At 240Hz, the brightness fluctuation repeats 240 times per second; at 14,880Hz, it repeats almost 15,000 times per second. That’s one hell of a difference. The reported modulation frequency of the new MacBook Pro’s OLED panel is roughly 62 times lower than that measured on the Mini-LED model.[1]

Frequency isn’t the only consideration, though. The extent to which brightness fluctuates during each cycle also matters, as do the characteristics of the display’s dimming system. We shouldn’t assume that these figures translate directly into how comfortable somebody will find a particular display. There’s no simple, one-size-fits-all formula for predicting who will experience problems.

It’s also worth avoiding the temptation to treat PWM as a universal explanation for every headache or instance of eye strain. Screen discomfort can have numerous causes. Some users’ discomfort may have nothing to do with PWM.[2]

Wait, isn’t OLED supposed to be better?

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is emphatically not an inexpensive laptop with a budget screen. This is Apple’s flagship professional notebook. The PROLED XDR configuration represents a substantial investment, and the display is arguably its most important selling point. Apple has spent years refining its displays, and there’s a reasonable expectation that moving to OLED should represent some sort of improvement in almost every meaningful respect, especially given the savagely high price tag of these new machines.

PWM isn’t exclusive to OLED. LCD displays can use it, too, including Mini-LED displays. The difference is that OLED panels often use PWM as part of their brightness-control behaviour, and manufacturers have considerable flexibility in how they implement it. Some OLED displays use relatively high-frequency modulation; others use a combination of PWM and DC (Direct Current) dimming to manage brightness.

DC dimming generally involves reducing the current supplied to the display rather than relying entirely on rapidly switching the light output on and off. It’s often considered preferable for people who are sensitive to PWM. But the presence of DC dimming doesn’t necessarily mean PWM has been eliminated. The new MacBook Pro appears to use a combination of PWM and DC dimming. Notebookcheck notes that DC dimming is present across brightness levels, but that the panel still exhibits 240Hz flickering.

The people who didn’t have a problem before

One of the problems with PWM discussions is that they tend to quickly become highly polarised. Someone says they experience headaches, and someone else responds that they’ve been using OLED displays for years without any issues. Two things can be true at once.

The most important aspect of this discussion, to me, is the number of people insisting they had no difficulty using OLED devices prior to using this new MacBook. This matters because PWM sensitivity is often discussed as though it’s a straightforward, binary distinction between people who can tolerate OLED and people who can’t. That binary distinction doesn’t exist. Sensitivity exists along a spectrum.

Different displays use different modulation frequencies, amplitudes and dimming characteristics. Two OLED panels can behave differently, even if they’re based on broadly similar technology. Someone who has been happily using an OLED iPhone Pro for several years might find a different OLED screen uncomfortable; someone who has experienced headaches with one OLED laptop might have absolutely no problem with another. And there is a distinction between OLED technology itself and the particular implementation of OLED in this particular MacBook.

To give an example, someone on the PWM_Sensitive subreddit posted this about their experience with the new MacBook Pro (shared with their permission):

I was really surprised I was affected by this. Have been looking at various OLED screens for years and did not expect to have issues.

Then I got my PROLED 16 inch last week and during the first few hours I thought I just had a bad day. Now it’s so obvious. As soon as I look at the screen I get lightheaded, I feel like I am floating away … and when I then get up and start walking, I feel dizzy for like an hour or two, then it gets better again. But as soon as I look at the screen for more than a minute, the dizziness comes back.

This is first machine in 20 years as an Apple customer that I return literally anything. Too bad, because the laptop is amazing in all aspects otherwise, I was in love with it the moment I took it out of the box (coming from an M1 Pro 16 inch). It would have been my daily driver for the next 5 years. So, now I am waiting for the M7 variant and hope they will find a way to mitigate this issue. I am returning the MacBook tomorrow morning after less than a week of using it.

Apple has built up a loyal audience of professional Mac users who spend enormous amounts of money on the machines, and enormous amounts of time in front of their displays. Photographers, designers, developers, writers and video editors can spend entire working days looking at a MacBook screen (I do). So imagine upgrading from an M4 or M5 Pro MacBook Pro with Mini-LED, expecting a more beautiful version of something you already love, only to discover that you can’t comfortably use the new machine for more than a short period. Good customer experience is usually Apple's guiding North Star. Bad customer experience is usually Apple’s Kryptonite.

Has Apple compromised on the wrong thing?

There are plenty of engineering considerations involved in developing a tandem OLED panel for a laptop — brightness, power consumption, thermal management, longevity, colour accuracy and uniformity all have to be balanced.

Apple's displays have always involved trade-offs to one degree or another. Take the Mini-LED display — while it's truly excellent in many respects, it notoriously suffers from blooming (an inherent limitation of Mini-LED local dimming) and has also typically had poor pixel response times. These are compromises Apple has had to accept in order to deliver the particular combination of brightness, contrast and HDR performance that makes the Mini-LED display so impressive.

Apple has made some ambitious claims about the new PROLED XDR display, particularly around its brightness and the intelligence of its display engine. We don’t know why Apple has ended up with this particular dimming behaviour, or what trade-offs were involved in achieving it. But I think it’s reasonable to ask whether display comfort received enough consideration in the process. The new MacBook Pro produces extraordinary blacks, stunning HDR highlights and exceptionally accurate colours, and so on. But none of that matters particularly much if the person sitting in front of it develops a headache, or feels like they want to throw up when they're using it.

When the majority experience isn’t everyone’s experience

People experiencing unusual, poorly understood or relatively uncommon health problems have often found themselves struggling to be heard — they have to explain their symptoms repeatedly, defend their experiences and convince others that their difficulties are genuine. I don't personally know anybody who suffers from PWM sensitivity, and I appreciate that it can be difficult for someone without these experiences to understand how something so ordinary could become a source of physical discomfort for another person. But personal experience shouldn't be a prerequisite for compassion. We don’t need to experience somebody else’s symptoms to acknowledge that they are struggling.

Stories like this tend to surface only once an ill-defined and arbitrary threshold of people complaining is crossed. But even if something only affects a small minority, doesn’t that minority matter? Apple certainly appears to care about the minority — they put an extraordinary amount of work into accessibility features, many of which are incredibly important to relatively small groups of users. It’s one of the things which sets Apple apart. Features such as VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch and other accessibility technologies exist because Apple recognises that different people interact with technology in different ways. Why shouldn’t display comfort receive similar consideration? It doesn’t mean Apple must abandon OLED, or compromise the experience for everyone. It means offering alternatives where technically feasible.

Apple previously introduced a ‘Display Pulse Smoothing option’ on supported iPhone models. It’s an accessibility setting which can be toggled in the Settings app. Apple describes Display Pulse Smoothing as a way to create a smoother dimming experience at low brightness on supported iPhones. Its support documentation cautions that disabling PWM may affect low-brightness display performance under certain conditions. It took Apple a long time to include this feature by the way (it arrived nearly 8 years after the iPhone X was released). Incidentally, Apple has also included Display Pulse Smoothing on the new iPad mini with OLED display.

Could something similar be offered on the Mac? We shouldn’t assume that a software feature would completely resolve the issue. Changing the way the display is driven could introduce other compromises, and Apple would need to implement it carefully. But even a degree of user control would be gratefully received.

For now, anyone concerned about PWM sensitivity should be cautious about buying the new machine without trying it first. A quick demo in an Apple Store isn’t necessarily representative of spending an entire working day in front of the display. Don’t assume that being comfortable with an OLED iPhone means you’ll be comfortable with this MacBook. If you experience discomfort, don’t assume that increasing brightness or changing colour settings will necessarily resolve it.

The existing Mini-LED MacBook Pro thankfully remains a viable alternative for people who have found that display comfortable. But the Mini-LED MacBook Pro might not stay around for much longer. Apple looks to be transitioning to OLED across their devices — this may have consequences unless Apple changes the way they're implementing this particular technology.

The best MacBook display isn’t necessarily the best display for everyone

We sometimes get so caught up in the pursuit of better specifications that we forget what these devices are actually for. The most important part of a display is that it's something you sit in front of for hours at a time.

Displays to my mind are like mattresses — they're not something you should compromise on, unless financial constraints demand it. I've often been puzzled why people baulk at paying a lot for a display when they’re likely going to be using it for several hours a day. Similarly, I’ve often wondered why people baulk at paying a lot of money for a mattress, when they’re going to be spending roughly a third of their lives lying on one. A decent mattress is probably something you should invest in. The specs of the mattress matter, of course, and individual comfort matters enormously. The same thing is true with a display, which is why I have no issue having spent the money I did on a Studio Display XDR.

And this is what's so problematic with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display. According to many reviewers this is one of the best displays they've ever seen, and it has a price to match. Starting at £2899 for the 14-inch version (£3399 for the 16-inch), boy is it expensive. If the technology responsible for making the PROLED XDR Display look spectacular also makes it uncomfortable for some people to use, then we need to ask if that trade-off is worth it.

I suspect most people buying the new MacBook Pro will never think about PWM. They’ll open the lid, admire the display and get on with their lives. But for the people who have discovered that they can no longer comfortably use the latest MacBook Pro, this is a really big deal.

I’d like to see Apple explain why the new display behaves so differently from the Mini-LED panel used in other MacBook Pro models, and whether there’s any possibility of improving its dimming characteristics through software. Perhaps there’s a perfectly reasonable engineering explanation. Perhaps there are limitations inherent in this particular panel.

I’d be interested to hear from anyone who has experienced this first-hand, particularly those who have previously used Apple’s OLED iPhones or iPads without difficulty, but are now struggling with the new MacBook Pro.

Get in touch at hello@macanorak.com

You can also submit feedback to Apple here: https://www.apple.com/feedback/macbook-pro/

A 62-fold difference in frequency doesn’t translate into a 62-fold difference in comfort. It doesn’t work that way. Frequency, modulation depth and individual sensitivity all matter. ↩︎

It may have to do with what type of screen they’ve opted for — glossy, or nano-texture. A personal example here: I have the nano-texture screen on the MacBook Pro, my iPad Pro and my iPhone Duo, and I get along with those just fine. But I could not get along with nano-texture on Apple's range of Studio Displays — it caused me a lot of visual discomfort / headaches — moving to glossy screens with those monitors has treated me much better in that regard. ↩︎

entry.title: Things That Turbo Pascal Is Smaller Than (2011)
entry.content:
It's not about technology for its own sake. It's about being able to implement your ideas.

Turbo Pascal 3 for MS-DOS was released in September 1986. Being version 3, there were lesser releases prior to it and flashier ones after, but 3 was a solid representation of the Turbo Pascal experience: a full Pascal compiler, including extensions that it made it practical for commercial use, tightly integrated with an editor. And the whole thing was lightning fast, orders of magnitude faster at building projects than Microsoft's compilers.

The entire Turbo Pascal 3.02 executable--the compiler and IDE--was 39,731 bytes. How does that stack up in 2011 terms? Here are some things that Turbo Pascal is smaller than, as of October 30, 2011:

The minified version of jquery 1.6 (90,518 bytes).

The yahoo.com home page (219,583 bytes).

The image of the white iPhone 4S at apple.com (190,157 bytes).

zlib.h in the Mac OS X Lion SDK (80,504 bytes).

The touch command under OS X Lion (44,016 bytes).

Various vim quick reference cards as PDFs. (This one is 47,508 bytes.)

The compiled code for the Erlang R14B02 parser (erl_parse.beam, 286,324 bytes).

The Wikipedia page for C++ (214,251 bytes).

entry.title: Show HN: db-branch – database branches in seconds for AI agents and CI, via ZFS
entry.content:
Instant database branches for MySQL and PostgreSQL, on your own servers.

Test a migration, let an AI agent loose, or give every pull request its own copy of the database. db-branch creates a copy-on-write branch of a large database in seconds, with nothing copied. Break it, reset it, throw it away. Built on ZFS clones, self-hosted, Apache-2.0.

Status: Beta. db-branch is usable today, but APIs and command-line details may still change before 1.0. It is an independent open-source project, built from scratch.

In your browser, 0 minutes. A live console demo runs entirely in the page (nothing real is created): https://demo.db-branch.com/

On a Mac or Windows machine, about 2 minutes. db-branch needs Linux and ZFS, so run it in an Ubuntu VM with Multipass. One command makes the VM, installs db-branch, initialises it on a file-backed ZFS pool and loads a small sample base, shop (MySQL 8.4):

multipass launch 24.04 --name db-branch-eval --memory 4G --disk 30G --timeout 900 \ --cloud-init https://raw.githubusercontent.com/db-branch/db-branch/main/scripts/eval-cloud-init.yaml multipass exec db-branch-eval -- cloud-init status --wait # wait for the setup (about two minutes) multipass exec db-branch-eval -- cat /etc/motd # console URL and sign-in (admin / admin), or what failed multipass shell db-branch-eval # then: sudo db-branch branch create try --base shop --ttl 1h --record

On Windows (PowerShell or cmd), put the multipass launch command on one line and drop the \:

multipass launch 24.04 --name db-branch-eval --memory 4G --disk 30G --timeout 900 --cloud-init https://raw.githubusercontent.com/db-branch/db-branch/main/scripts/eval-cloud-init.yaml The history module is turned on, and the paid modules run for 30 days without a key. --record records a branch so it can be restored to any point. The pool is a file, so it is slower and not meant for real data. The first admin password is admin; the console asks for a new one at the first sign-in. On Apple Silicon (and other arm64 machines) the setup downloads about 800 MB for MySQL, against 80 MB on Intel, because Oracle ships no minimal build for arm64. --timeout 900 keeps launch from giving up on a slow connection. If the setup fails, /etc/motd says so, and sudo tail -n 30 /var/log/cloud-init-output.log in the VM shows why. Delete the VM with multipass delete --purge db-branch-eval.

On your own Ubuntu server. See Install.

 AI agent sandboxes. The built-in MCP server lets an LLM agent create a branch, run a risky query or migration on it, and delete the branch, so production data is never touched. A database per pull request. Each CI run or PR gets its own copy of a large database, ready in seconds, and removed by --ttl when it is no longer needed. Version-upgrade checks. Run a major-version upgrade (for example MySQL 8.0 to 8.4) on one branch first, with branch upgrade --check-only to see what it would run into, before touching the base. Branches in seconds. On our own 3-node test cluster a PostgreSQL branch is ready in about 0.5 s and a MySQL branch in about 3 s, with 0 bytes copied at creation (copy-on-write). Reset and expire. branch reset returns a branch to its creation state; --ttl deletes it automatically. Checkpoints. branch checkpoint saves a running branch's state instantly; branch restore puts it back. Restoring replaces the current state, and every checkpoint you already have stays restorable. Per-branch upgrades. branch upgrade moves one branch to a newer MySQL or PostgreSQL version while the base and the other branches stay put. A checkpoint is saved first, and a failed upgrade rolls back by itself. MySQL and PostgreSQL, several versions at once. Engine runtimes are installed by version and can live side by side. One interface everywhere. CLI, REST API, web console and an MCP server (so LLM agents can create and query their own branches) all use the same API. Single node or cluster. A Raft cluster of VMs, with optional ProxySQL routing so applications keep one address.

Requirements: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or 26.04 LTS, and a ZFS pool (the zfsutils-linux package is installed as a dependency).

curl -fsSL https://apt.db-branch.com/db-branch.gpg | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/db-branch.gpg >/dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/db-branch.gpg] https://apt.db-branch.com stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/db-branch.list sudo apt update && sudo apt install db-branch sudo db-branch init --pool <zpool>

The repository signing key fingerprint is 3F404C4E5D49FA653F8385692C6E89E341D4D7A5. db-branch init prints the initial admin password once.

db-branch runtime install postgres@18.6 # a database engine version db-branch base create prod --runtime postgres@18.6 --dump prod.sql.gz # a base: your data, loaded once db-branch branch create feature-x --base prod --ttl 72h # a branch: instant, copy-on-write db-branch branch dsn feature-x # connection URL (includes the password) db-branch branch checkpoint feature-x --name before-migration # save the state (instant) db-branch branch restore feature-x before-migration # go back to the saved state db-branch branch reset feature-x # discard every change db-branch branch delete feature-x # remove it

MySQL works the same way, for example mysql@8.4.13. List installable versions with db-branch runtime available. To try a version upgrade on one MySQL branch:

db-branch branch upgrade feature-x --runtime mysql@8.4.13 --check-only # what would the upgrade run into? db-branch branch upgrade feature-x --runtime mysql@8.4.13 # move this branch only; a checkpoint is saved first

A base is a ZFS dataset holding a loaded database. A branch is a ZFS clone of a base snapshot, so creating one copies nothing, and each branch runs its own database server on its own port. Optionally, ProxySQL routes client connections to the right branch by user name (or by a /*db_branch='name'*/ query comment). Several nodes form a Raft cluster that shares bases, branches, settings and users.

Core (this repository), Apache-2.0: branches, bases, runtimes, clustering, CLI, API, web console, MCP, monitoring, notifications, anonymous (no sign-in) branches with limits, scheduled base refresh, backup of cluster state. Free modules in the same apt repository: proxysql, greenmask, greenmask-mysql, anon (routing and data masking). Paid modules (auth/SSO, audit, history, diff, FSx storage) are separate, closed-source packages, self-hosted and enabled with a license key (monthly or yearly). A governed masking workflow is planned as an opt-in beta and is not part of any plan yet. See docs/modules.md for the extension points they use.

There is no hosted or cloud version of db-branch.

docs/README.md: index of the design and reference documents (written in Japanese) English user documentation: https://db-branch.com/docs/ Website: https://db-branch.com (English), https://db-branch.com/ja/ (Japanese) api/openapi.yaml: machine-readable REST API definition CHANGELOG.md Contributions are welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md. Commits need a DCO sign-off (git commit -s). Security issues: see SECURITY.md. Please use private vulnerability reporting, not public issues. Support: see SUPPORT.md. No support is promised; Issues are read when possible. Please follow the Code of Conduct.

Apache-2.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE.

db-branch は、ZFS クローンで MySQL / PostgreSQL のデータベースブランチを発行・リセット・破棄するツールです。現在は Beta で、1.0 までに API が変わる可能性があります。コアは Apache-2.0 で、有償モジュール（認証/SSO・監査・履歴・差分・FSx ストレージ）は別パッケージ（クローズドソース、セルフホスト、ライセンスキー）です。

Mac / Windows では、Multipass のコマンド1つで試せます: https://db-branch.com/ja/docs/getting-started/#multipass-ですぐ試す。日本語のサイトは https://db-branch.com/ja/、設計ドキュメントは docs/ にあります（日本語）。

entry.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
entry.content:
All AI-generated code should be Open Source

This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.

First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.

The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.

However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.

Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.

entry.title: Emacs Is My Browser
entry.content:
In my ever-increasing desire to use emacs as my sole computing environment, I have started to take browsing the web inside it far more seriously. Where I previously had thought EWW to be a niceity but far from capable, after using it for a few days it seems to be useable for about 85-90% of use cases - even on the javascript riddled hellhole that is the internet.

Why?#

I have seen in my own use of the modern browser (chromium/firefox) that it is far too easy to get distracted - too easy to get off track and fall down rabbit holes that take over my day. There are infinite suggestions as to how I should spend my time, uncountable shiny objects that take my eye off the prize that is Creativity and Depth. This has been momentously negated with EWW (or any terminal browser, lynx or browsh for the non-emacs users).

In addition to this, my belief is that we should make strides toward leaving behind Layer 8 of the internet - the limiting frontends of social platforms and locked away corners of the net that limit actual discourse (Discord, I’m looking at you). We have given up far too much to big tech platforms, and gotten nothing of value in return, to the point that many now think the internet is dying.

The internet is just a delivery mechanism, and for people that see it for what it really is, the internet has never been more alive. I truly recommend using the internet as if it was 1999.

Even on my phone, I’ve stopped using javascript frontends and embraced using eww in emacs (in termux), only falling back to fennec for about 5-10% of usecases:

I find this way of using the internet far higher in signal than any other method, allowing me to look up information, read documentation, and produce more.

How I am doing this#

For the uninitiated, emacs ships with EWW (Emacs Web Wowser) permitting you to browse the web with image and gif (when did gifs die, I almost never see them these days!) support directly inside Emacs.

I have some sane defaults that permit ease of use such as using B for back, U for yanking url at point, and a few built in functions.

Hitting R will invoke eww readable which is similar to reader mode in firefox, removing headers and footers and focusing in on the text on page. Useful.

You can send the page to your default browser with &. If a page doesn’t render nicely, this is a good fallback.

D will download images locally, b goes back a page, a will save bookmarks. All of this makes browsing in eww truly enjoyable.

I have also set .pdf to open in emacs, .mp4 and youtube/video hosting links to open in mpv, and gopher/gemini links to open in elpher. Elpher is the EWW for the gopher and gemini protocols, the smolweb that is all signal and no noise.

EWW uses Shr to render html, so you will see some callouts to that in my configuration below:

My browser.el setup:#

Here’s how I have configured EWW to work in my Emacs configuration:

My default search engine is my own Searx instance, a privacy respecting frontend that amalgamates all other search engines.

Limitations#

You will not be watching youtube videos or reading Tweets (x.com is adversarial to non-JS supported browsers). You will not be using social media, nor will you be logging into any platforms. You will not be doing your online banking, filling in government forms, or viewing client portals.

The usecase is quick web searches, documentation, and reading blogs generally. Once more, hitting & in any web page will bring up your default browser to continue your session in chromium or firefox when you do run into pages that don’t work well in EWW.

Conclusion#

I have reverted all my url functions to default to browsing in EWW, so any web interaction must first go through EWW. This has encouraged me to deeply consider what I am doing online first and foremost, and then only falling back to a modern browser when needed. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much I am able to do inside emacs, and continue to move toward using it as my computing environment in perpetuity.

As always, God bless, and until next time.
